findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the concrete 'small spend floor' (a dollar value or a rule) used to select days for the threshold median.
evidence: 'the median, over the same window and over days above a small spend floor, of (undimensioned tokens x CEILING) divided by the CE Bedrock total'
The floor selects the day-set feeding the median that sets the enforcement threshold, so it is load-bearing for the shipped value.
findings.finding: The threshold derivation depends on a 'small spend floor' that filters which UTC days enter the median, but the floor value is never specified.
scenarios: An executor deriving the threshold picks an arbitrary floor and produces a different threshold than intended.
Very-low-spend idle days would otherwise skew the ratio median.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 'a small spend floor' with an explicit figure, e.g. 'CE Bedrock total above $X for that UTC day', since figures are said to be derivable.

bedrock_spend_cap.tf:334-339 grants Action = [ce:GetCostAndUsage, cloudwatch:ListMetrics, cloudwatch:GetMetricData]
cloudwatch:ListMetrics is referenced only in this grant (search_files: single hit at :336)
'No unused Terraform declarations remain. Checked: terraform validate' — validate does not catch an unused-but-syntactically-valid IAM action

scenarios: After deploy the Lambda no longer calls ListMetrics, yet its role retains the permission — least-privilege drift that outlives the pricing-layer deletion the plan is otherwise cleaning up.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the "cloudwatch:ListMetrics" entry from the ReadSpendSignals statement's Action list, leaving ce:GetCostAndUsage and cloudwatch:GetMetricData.

handler.py:72 `from typing import Literal`; handler.py:311 `RateSource = Literal[...]` is the only `Literal` use, and RateSource is on the removal list.
findings.finding: The Python removal inventory omits two module-level imports that become orphaned once the enumerated symbols go: `import re` (handler.py:70) is referenced only inside `_normalise` (line 204) and `_strip_billing_region` (line 209), both on the removal list; `from typing import Literal` (handler.py:72) is referenced only by the `RateSource` alias (line 311), also on the removal list. No AC covers Python unused-import cleanup — the 'No unused Terraform declarations' criterion is Terraform-only.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'The seven pricing functions ... and six constants ... are absent' and 'state["rates"] ... MeteredRate and its RateSource alias ... are removed'
scenarios: After removal, `import re` at handler.py:70 is unused — an orphaned reference the inventory does not name.
After removal, `from typing import Literal` at handler.py:72 is unused — an orphaned reference the inventory does not name.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the last AC to require that `import re` and `from typing import Literal` are removed once their sole consumers are deleted, verified by `make lint` reporting no unused imports.

findings.checklist_item: Route the zero-dimension-aggregate-series assumption through a SPIKE that re-confirms, per enforced region via a live GetMetricData read, that each of the four AWS/Bedrock token metrics returns an undimensioned series equal to the per-ModelId sum, before deleting the per-ModelId read path — and record the probe as the drift guard the plan already alludes to.
evidence: CloudWatch does not universally auto-publish zero-dimension rollups; the same MetricName with a ModelId dimension is a distinct metric from one with no dimensions, so the aggregate exists only if AWS/Bedrock explicitly emits it
The plan's evidence is a one-off 11-day observation, not a docs citation or a repeatable check an executor can run before committing
AC 'issues exactly four undimensioned GetMetricData queries per region' and 'calls no list_metrics' hard-depend on this surface existing
EVIDENCE CLASS: Partially-verified — the vendor/endpoint (GetMetricData on AWS/Bedrock) is in use, but the specific zero-dimension surface + equality-to-sum property is unconfirmed
findings.finding: The redesign's core mechanism — that AWS/Bedrock publishes a zero-dimension (undimensioned) aggregate series per token metric via GetMetricData that exactly equals the sum of the per-ModelId series — is an external-capability assertion grounded only in a single private observation window (2026-09-14..09-24), not in docs or a repeatable probe, yet the plan deletes the per-ModelId read path that is today the only proven signal.
findings.location: Approach section: 'AWS/Bedrock does publish a zero-dimension series per token metric; over 2026-09-14 to 09-24 it equalled the sum of the per-ModelId series exactly'
scenarios: AWS/Bedrock stops or never actually emits the aggregate series in one enforced region, so an undimensioned GetMetricData returns empty while real spend flows — the estimate reads zero and the cap never trips
The aggregate diverges from the per-ModelId sum after the deletion, and there is no per-ModelId fallback left to reconcile against

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the high-water mark's per-UTC-day reset (when it returns to zero at the day boundary and who writes that) and the atomicity/ownership of its read-modify-write under overlapping ticks, plus an AC covering the day-rollover reset.
evidence: 'the handler persists the day's highest observed token total: an empty read may release only when no earlier tick that UTC day observed tokens'

'An all-empty read with no earlier nonzero reading that UTC day may release' vs '...after an earlier nonzero reading that day holds the deny' — both hinge on a per-day mark whose day-rollover reset and concurrent-update semantics are unstated
ABSENCE: no CREATE-at-day-start / RETIRE-at-day-boundary rule and no atomicity statement for the mark's update
findings.finding: The plan introduces a persisted per-UTC-day high-water mark ('the day's highest observed token total') that the release discriminator depends on, but does not specify its RETIRE/reset path at the UTC-day boundary nor the concurrency/ownership of its read-modify-write. Without a stated reset, a prior day's nonzero mark would hold the deny into a fresh idle day (defeating the automatic release the plan is built to preserve); without atomic update semantics, overlapping ticks can race on the mark.
findings.location: Approach — 'Release discriminator' paragraph; ACs on empty-read release/hold
findings.suggested_fix: State that the persisted mark is keyed by UTC day (or reset when the observed UTC day changes) so a new day starts at zero, and describe the state write as a single atomic put (or CAS) per tick; add a test that a prior-day nonzero mark does not hold the deny on the next UTC day.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: Specify the default the release discriminator assumes when the persisted high-water key is absent (e.g. from old-handler state), and ensure a mid-day deploy with a deny attached does not release on a first-tick empty read.
evidence: Plan AC: 'The first tick after deploy tolerates state written by the old handler, ignoring its rate keys.'
Plan: 'an empty read may release only when no earlier tick that UTC day observed tokens.'
Old state document (handler.py:608-613) has no high-water key; absent key defaults to the release-eligible branch.
findings.finding: The 'first tick after deploy tolerates old state' criterion and the release discriminator are not reconciled for a mid-day deploy. Pre-change state carries no high-water key, so a first-tick empty read would be classified as 'no earlier nonzero that day' and become release-eligible — even if a deny is attached from a genuine earlier trip that same UTC day. The initial/default value of the persisted high-water mark when absent from old state is unspecified.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'The first tick after deploy tolerates state written by the old handler' vs 'an all-empty read … may release'
scenarios: Deploy lands mid-UTC-day while the deny is attached from a real earlier trip; old state lacks the high-water key; first tick sees a transient empty CloudWatch read and, finding no persisted prior-nonzero, releases the deny prematurely.
findings.suggested_fix: On a missing high-water key, seed it from the current attachment state or from CE's last reading rather than treating absence as 'no tokens seen today', so an attached deny is not released by a transient empty read on the first post-deploy tick.

findings.checklist_item: State the exact GetMetricData MetricStat shape for the undimensioned read (Dimensions key omitted, or the confirmed equivalent) and assert it in a test, so the four aggregate queries are proven to select the aggregate series rather than an empty one.
evidence: The current handler builds MetricStat.Metric.Dimensions from list_metrics results (handler.py lines 424-432); the new path removes list_metrics but the plan never states how the undimensioned Metric block is formed

A MetricStat targeting the ModelId-dimensioned series returns different data than one with no Dimensions key; flag/parameter-level empiricism (Dimensions omitted vs empty list) is exactly the class T3 flags as silent-runtime-failure risk
findings.finding: The plan specifies the count of undimensioned queries ('exactly four undimensioned GetMetricData queries per region') but not the parameter-level mechanics of expressing an undimensioned MetricStat, i.e. whether the query omits Dimensions entirely or sends Dimensions: []; these are not equivalent to CloudWatch and choosing wrong silently returns no data.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria: '_metered_spend issues exactly four undimensioned GetMetricData queries per region'
scenarios: The executor sends Dimensions: [] where AWS expects the key absent (or vice versa) and GetMetricData returns an empty series, reproducing the fail-open under-read

findings.checklist_item: State whether the high-water-mark 'gap' classification also fails closed on the TRIP decision when no deny is attached (empty read after a prior nonzero that day), or explicitly justify why CE alone is the accepted backstop for that case.
evidence: Plan: 'an empty read may release only when no earlier tick that UTC day observed tokens; once a nonzero total has been seen, a later empty read is a gap and the deny is held.'
handler.py:466-467 current fail-closed: `if failures and not contributed: return None` → handler sets `spend = THRESHOLD_USD`
Plan: 'CE lags 8-24h and reads zero for hours into a busy day.'
findings.finding: The persisted high-water-mark discriminator is specified only for the release decision ('may release'/'holds the deny'), presupposing a deny already exists. It is silent on the trip side: when no deny is attached and a mid-day CloudWatch gap returns an all-empty read, the ceiling estimate under-reads to 0 and enforcement relies solely on Cost Explorer, which the plan itself says lags 8-24h. Today's handler fails closed to THRESHOLD on a metered gap (`metered is None`); the new mechanism appears to drop that fail-closed-on-gap for the unattached case.
scenarios: Deny not yet attached; a runaway is in progress; the undimensioned GetMetricData momentarily returns empty (metrics-publishing gap) after an earlier nonzero read that day; ceiling estimate is 0 and CE has not yet caught up, so the tick neither trips nor holds.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a clause: when an all-empty read follows an earlier nonzero reading that UTC day, treat metered spend as at least the persisted high-water estimate (a floor) for BOTH the trip and the hold-release decisions, not only the release decision.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the 'AWS/Bedrock publishes a zero-dimension aggregate token series' capability assertion against a documented AWS source (or state it as account-observed with a drift guard that alarms if the undimensioned Sum ever diverges from the summed per-ModelId series).
evidence: Retrieved (educative.io): AWS/Bedrock metrics are 'broken down by the ModelId dimension'

Retrieved (cdklabs generative-ai-cdk-constructs): 'Native runtime metrics for Amazon Bedrock don't support dimensions beyond model ID' — describes query-time aggregation across workloads, not a separately-published undimensioned series
No retrieved source affirms a distinct zero-dimension aggregate series is published; the plan grounds the equality only in an account-specific window
findings.finding: The entire approach depends on the load-bearing capability claim that AWS/Bedrock publishes a zero-dimension aggregate series per token metric equal to the sum of the per-ModelId series, but this is resolved only by an account-specific 11-day observation (2026-09-14 to 09-24), not by any documented AWS capability. Retrieved AWS/community sources describe AWS/Bedrock token metrics only as ModelId-dimensioned.
findings.location: Approach section: "AWS/Bedrock does publish a zero-dimension series per token metric; over 2026-09-14 to 09-24 it equalled the sum of the per-ModelId series exactly"
scenarios: A future Bedrock metric change, or a ModelId series that lacks a matching undimensioned rollup, silently under-counts the fast signal and lets the cap fire late
Reviewer cannot confirm the aggregate-vs-per-model equality holds outside the 11-day sample

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cite and contrast the chosen ceiling-pricing approach against the AWS/Jamf 'Tokenomics at scale' prior art (per-model published rates + explicit pricing branch), justifying why the unbounded-over-estimate ceiling is preferred here over the established per-model-rate pattern.
evidence: Retrieved: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/tokenomics-at-scale-how-jamf-built-real-time-spend-enforcement-for-amazon-bedrock/ — 'real-time, per-user spend enforcement for Amazon Bedrock using ... a serverless AWS Lambda loop'
Retrieved: github.com/jamf/bedrock-spend-enforcement — 'Tiered, real-time' Bedrock spend controls, companion to the AWS blog

Retrieved (aiunderstanding.org summary of the AWS post): 'AWS instructs adopters to ... add an explicit pricing branch whenever a new model is enabled' — the same mechanism the plan proposes as its fallback `{ModelId: rate}` override
Plan cites no prior art or alternatives-considered for the chosen architecture despite arguing the opposite rate strategy to the AWS-published one
findings.finding: The plan chooses a novel ceiling-pricing architecture and deletes the empirical per-model rate layer without considering the directly relevant, current prior art: AWS's 'Tokenomics at scale: How Jamf built real-time spend enforcement for Amazon Bedrock' (Sep 2026 blog + jamf/bedrock-spend-enforcement repo), a near-identical serverless-Lambda + IAM-deny Bedrock spend enforcement system that advocates per-model published rates with an explicit pricing branch per model. Notably the plan's own fallback remedy (a `{ModelId: rate}` exact-match override) reinvents that AWS-recommended 'explicit pricing branch,' yet the tradeoff between the two rate strategies is never made against the established pattern.
findings.location: Approach section ("Delete the pricing-derivation layer") and Accepted limitation ("the remedy if it bites is an exact-match {ModelId: rate} override")
scenarios: Reviewer/executor cannot tell whether ceiling-pricing was chosen over the AWS-recommended per-model-rate pattern deliberately or in ignorance of it
The 'accepted limitation' (unbounded over-estimate for cheap/cache-free models) is exactly the failure mode the AWS pattern's explicit per-model branch avoids
findings.suggested_fix: Add an 'Alternatives considered' note referencing the AWS 'Tokenomics at scale' blog and jamf/bedrock-spend-enforcement repo; state explicitly that the deferred `{ModelId: rate}` override is the AWS-recommended per-model branch, and justify shipping the ceiling first (simplicity, fail-closed) over adopting per-model rates up front.
